column3: Equivalence — police officers' salaries
column4: 255,000 police officers
column5: 245,000 police officers
column6: The police-officer equivalence divided a year of subsidy by a constable's pay that was out of date: £48,231, the 2024 rate. The pay award of 1 September 2025 raised it to £50,256, so the same year of subsidy pays fewer officers. The count fell from 255,000 to 245,000. Recorded retrospectively on 10 October 2026 from the public repository history (commit 51d10136).

column3: Emissions trading (power-sector share of UK auction revenue)
column6: The power sector's share of UK ETS emissions was taken as 30.4 of 85.6 MtCO2e. No published source gives 30.4 Mt: DESNZ's Functioning of the UK carbon market, 2024 (section 7.3) gives 29,484,524 tCO2e of 85,634,344, a share of 34.43% rather than 35.51%. The 2022 denominator was likewise held as 110.0 Mt against a published 110.6 Mt, and 2023 was held at the 2023 report's 37.1 Mt after DESNZ restated it to 36,084,695 tCO2e. Revenue for 2024 now uses the published calendar-year auction total (£2,564,090,000 across 25 auctions) instead of converting a financial-year accounts figure. 2022 and 2023 also move, to £2,635.4m and £1,270.7m. Found during routine checking of this site's figures against primary sources.

column3: Balancing costs (BSUoS uplift)
column4: £12.54bn cumulative (£1.62bn/yr run-rate)
column5: £22.85bn cumulative (£3.39bn/yr run-rate)
column6: The series was built from NESO's Daily Balancing Costs dataset, which is a breakdown of balancing-mechanism and ancillary spend rather than the balancing cost recovered through BSUoS. Its columns sum to 23-39% below the outturn in NESO's Annual Balancing Costs Report in every year from 2018-19 (2023-24: £1,824m against £2,455m). Two faults compounded. The dataset is narrower than the charge it was taken to represent; and the fetched series began on 1 April 2017, so the published 2017 figure covered nine months rather than twelve. Together they produced a 63% fall between raw 2016 (£1,200m) and raw 2017 (£439m). On the corrected basis the missing quarter accounts for 26% of calendar 2017, and the narrow basis understated the nine months actually fetched by a further 52%. The series now reads NESO's settled BSUoS charge data: the half-hourly charge to 31 March 2023, and actual BSUoS cost thereafter, the fixed-tariff reform of April 2023 having broken the identity between what users are charged and what balancing costs. Both are on the gross BSUoS basis, matching the pre-2017 history and the £0.4bn/yr 2002-05 baseline. The corrected series runs 1.10-1.23 times the Annual Balancing Costs Report outturn with no step at either seam, and the 2016-to-2017 change is +3.2%. The combined total in 2024 prices rises from £228.6bn to £239.9bn; the published headline of over £220 billion is unchanged. The error understated the cost, so the correction raises the figure. Found while checking this site's own figures against primary sources during a review of a Renewable Energy Foundation paper.

column3: Headline total — how it was described
column4: described as payments to generators
column5: stated as including estimated indirect costs
column6: The headline counter includes the estimated indirect costs — network and balancing charges, carbon pricing and the capacity levy — whenever the 'Include indirect costs' switch is on, which is its default. The sentence printed directly beneath the figure named only the four direct schemes: the Renewables Obligation, Contracts for Difference, Feed-in Tariffs and constraint payments. Those four are £132.3bn of the £229.2bn shown. The remaining £96.9bn, about two pounds in every five, is the estimated indirect layer, and the caption did not say so. The figure itself was not wrong, and the switch controlling it was visible and correctly labelled. What was wrong was the description: a reader who took the caption as the definition of the number — the ordinary reading — would have understood a measured total of payments to generators, when more than two fifths of it is an attributed estimate. This site's own rule is that estimated and measured money must never be presented as the same thing. The cause was a display change of 18 June 2026. Two sentences that did carry the disclosure — 'including estimated indirect costs' above the figure, and 'plus estimated indirect system costs' below it — were written correctly but hidden by the stylesheet of the new page design, which replaced them with the shorter caption. From 23 June 2026, when the indirect switch began defaulting to on, the combined figure was published under a description of the direct schemes alone. It stood for 99 days. The caption now names the indirect costs in both states of the switch, and links to the attribution method. The methodology page has also been corrected: it stated that indirect costs were never folded into the headline, which was true of an earlier design and not of the one shipped. Found while reconciling this site against a review of a Renewable Energy Foundation paper.

column3: Equivalence — hospitals
column4: 120 of the largest new NHS hospitals
column5: England's entire New Hospital Programme (46 hospital schemes), 4 times over
column6: The hospital equivalence divided the full cost by £2bn, treated as the cost of one of the largest new NHS hospitals. The National Audit Office's figure is the bottom of its top cost band ('£2 billion or more'), not a typical cost, so 120 hospitals overstated what the money would buy. The programme's scheme costs also include future inflation, so they are not in today's money. The equivalence now divides by the NAO's £60bn total for the whole New Hospital Programme (46 schemes). Because that total includes future inflation, the count of 4 understates rather than overstates. Recorded retrospectively on 10 October 2026 from the public repository history (commit c9e4eb90).

column3: Equivalence — social homes
column4: 610,000 social homes
column5: 590,000 social homes
column6: The cost of one social home, £393,333 (Cebr: £35.4bn for 90,000 homes), is stated in 2023 prices. It was divided into a total in 2024 prices without first being brought up to 2024 prices, which overstated the number of homes by about 3%. Converted to 2024 prices, the count is 590,000. Recorded retrospectively on 10 October 2026 from the public repository history (commit 68c39523).

column3: Payments to switch wind farms off
column4: £2.670bn cumulative; £358m a year
column5: £2.631bn cumulative; £345m a year
column6: Switch-off payments since October 2023 were costed as volume times bid price. Elexon settles each payment at volume times price times a transmission loss multiplier, which scales a unit's metered output for losses on the grid in its zone. For wind farms in northern Scotland the multiplier is about 0.96, so leaving it out overstated the cost of switch-offs by 3.7–3.9% a year. The fault showed up in a check against the Renewable Energy Foundation's independent count. Volumes matched exactly (8.36 TWh in 2024, 10.24 TWh in 2025), but costs did not: £410.8m against £394.3m for 2024, and £397.4m against £382.1m for 2025. With the multiplier the figures are £395.7m and £382.1m. The combined headline does not move: the switch-off line is carried inside the balancing-cost total, so the £40m it loses returns to the balancing line it is split from.

column3: The full cost including estimated indirect costs (the large number on the front page)
column4: £233.0bn in today's money (2024 prices), shown as over £230 billion, from 13 October 2026 until this release (£240.8bn before the Capacity Market change of 13 October). The counter added an estimate only from the time the Clock was last built, not from the end of each source's latest data.
column5: £188.4bn to 31 December 2024, the total counted in Report No. 1, in today's money (2024 prices). The Clock runs on from there: the data published since add £11.9bn and an estimate of costs incurred but not yet published adds about £19.9bn, so the Clock read £220.2bn on 14 October 2026, and rising.
column6: The live Clock showed £233.0bn (2024 prices) from 13 October 2026, and £240.8bn before the Capacity Market change of that day. Corrections and changes of method, each listed separately in this log with its own effect and itemised in Technical Paper No. 1 (Annex F), bring the total over all published data, each line counted to its own latest official data, to £200.2bn in five steps. First, the grid and balancing costs of 2002 to 2005 that a Britain without net zero would have paid were taken from the model, not from rounded figures: £233.0bn to £227.0bn. Second, that cost was taken from the model year by year for every year: £227.0bn to £212.4bn. Third, the balancing costs were put on one basis, a 2021 grid charge was corrected, charges were put on calendar years, and the Climate Change Levy was counted only while renewable electricity was exempt from it (to 31 July 2015): £212.4bn to £201.2bn. Fourth, a review of the grid and balancing method, including the final 2005-06 Scottish grid figures: £201.2bn to £200.3bn. Fifth, two Feed-in Tariff scheme years that had been transposed were put back in Ofgem's order: £200.3bn to £200.2bn. The lines' latest data end on different dates: the daily and monthly lines run to within weeks of the release, the yearly ones only to December 2024 or March 2025. Report No. 1 therefore counts every line to 31 December 2024, the last date to which every line is published, with the Renewables Obligation and Feed-in Tariff scheme years (April to March) put on calendar years: £188.4bn (£188.37bn; £188.38bn before the Feed-in Tariff correction). The Clock runs on from that total. The data published since 31 December 2024 add £11.9bn (£11.88bn). The Clock now also counts the costs already incurred since each line's latest data but not yet published, carried forward at that line's latest annual rate: about £19.9bn (£19.93bn; £20.7bn in cash) at 14 October 2026. Together they take the Clock to £220.2bn on that date. The line under the counter shows the three parts. When a source publishes new figures they replace the estimate for that period, so nothing is counted twice. The year-by-year chart and tables still show published figures only. The method is the one in Technical Paper No. 1, section 8, which gives the same total, £220.17bn, for 14 October 2026.

column3: The cost per household a year, the cost a year and the cost a second, in today's money (the strip under the front-page counter)
column4: £633 per household a year (£633.16); £18.4bn a year (£18.36bn); £581.85 a second, in today's money (2024 prices), at 14 October 2026, after the headline correction above. Before this release the live Clock showed £708.33 per household and £20.5bn a year, on the old headline method.
column5: £649 per household a year (£649.42); £18.8bn a year (£18.83bn); £596.79 a second, in today's money (2024 prices), at 14 October 2026.
column6: The cost a year is the sum of each cost line's latest yearly rate. Those rates belong to different years: the Renewables Obligation and Feed-in Tariffs to April 2024 to March 2025, the Climate Change Levy, emissions trading and the grid charge to calendar 2024, and the daily and monthly lines to the twelve months to October 2026. To put the total in today's money (2024 prices), the Clock converted the whole sum with one year's price index, the 2025 one. That counted inflation twice on the lines already in 2024 money, about £12.8bn of the £19.1bn a year in cash, and so understated the cost a year by about £0.5bn. Each line is now converted from its own year's prices, and the lines are then added up. Lines already in 2024 money are left as they are. The cost a year moves from £18.36bn to £18.83bn, and the cost per household from £633 to £649 a year. The cost per second and per MWh move in step. The cumulative total is not affected: it was always converted year by year.
